string-array.name: risk_otp_theft
string-array.item: OTP theft / account takeover pattern
The app can receive SMS, including bank and WhatsApp one-time codes, and can reach the internet. Fake invitation, traffic-ticket and parcel APKs use this combination to take over accounts.

This pattern appears because SMS access comes together with concealment or untrusted-source signs (a hidden icon, a file from outside an app store, a debug or brand-new certificate, a luring name), or with code that sends SMS content out, a hidden destination or call forwarding.
The app\'s code has not been analysed yet, so it is not proven that SMS are read or sent anywhere. This assessment comes from the manifest and context only.
Do not install this file. If it is installed: revoke SMS permission, uninstall it, then change passwords and re-enable two-step verification for important accounts (WhatsApp, bank, email).

string-array.name: risk_screen_spying
string-array.item: Screen spying pattern
An accessibility service can read other apps\' screens, including messages, balances and typed text, and the app could send it over the internet.
This pattern appears because screen-reading accessibility comes together with other signs, such as a hidden icon, overlays, device admin, a notification listener or an untrusted source.
It is not proven that screen content is sent anywhere. The app\'s code has not been analysed yet.
Turn this app\'s accessibility service off in Settings → Accessibility unless you use it on purpose. Uninstall it if you do not recognise it.

string-array.name: risk_accessibility
string-array.item: Accessibility service
When enabled, it can read screen content and tap on the user\'s behalf.
Normal for screen readers, password managers, automation tools and alternative launchers.
Not proven that screen data leaves the device. Code not analysed yet.
Enable it only if you know what it is for. Check Settings → Accessibility.

string-array.name: risk_notifications
string-array.item: Notification listener
When enabled, the app can read every notification, including message text and one-time codes.
Normal for smartwatches, reminder apps and notification managers.
Not proven that notifications are stored or sent.
Allow it only for apps you trust. Check Settings → Notifications → Notification access.

string-array.name: risk_device_admin
string-array.item: Device admin
A device admin can lock the screen, change the screen lock or even erase data, and is hard to uninstall while active.
Normal for work (MDM), find-my-device and parental control apps.
Not proven that these policies are used.
Deactivate it in Settings → Security → Device admin apps if not needed.

string-array.name: risk_sms
string-array.item: SMS access
The app can receive or read SMS, including one-time codes.
Normal for SMS apps, some banking apps that auto-fill verification codes, and spam blockers.
Not proven that SMS are read or sent anywhere. Code not analysed yet.
If the app does not need SMS for its features, revoke the SMS permission in Settings → Apps.

string-array.name: risk_sms_send
string-array.item: Sending SMS
The app can send SMS from your number, which can cost money or spread links to your contacts.
Normal for SMS apps and some verification apps.
Not proven that any SMS was sent.
Revoke the SMS permission if not needed and check your sent messages.

string-array.name: risk_contacts_calls
string-array.item: Contacts and call history
The app can read your contact list or call history.
Normal for messaging, phone and contact backup apps.
Not proven that contact data leaves the device.
Revoke contacts or call log permission if unrelated to the app\'s purpose.

string-array.name: risk_phone_identity
string-array.item: Phone identity and accounts
The app can read phone state, your number or the accounts on the device.
Common in calling apps, games and analytics SDKs that tell devices apart.
Not proven that this data is sent.
Revoke the \"Phone\" permission if the app does not make calls.

string-array.name: risk_camera_mic
string-array.item: Camera and microphone
The app can use the camera or record audio once permitted.
Normal for photo, video, calling and QR apps. Android 12+ shows a green indicator while the camera or microphone is in use.
Not proven that recording happens in the background.
Choose \"Only while using the app\" or \"Ask every time\" for camera and microphone.

string-array.name: risk_location
string-array.item: Location
The app can know where you are; with background location, also while it is closed.
Normal for maps, ride-hailing, weather and find-my-device apps.
Not proven that location is sent or stored.
Use approximate location or \"Only while using the app\" where possible.

string-array.name: risk_screen_capture
string-array.item: Screen recording
The app can record or cast the whole screen after you accept Android\'s prompt.
Normal for screen recorders, meeting screen sharing and game streaming.
Android asks every time recording starts; not proven that anything was recorded.
Decline unexpected screen recording prompts, especially while opening banking apps.

string-array.name: risk_overlay
string-array.item: Display over other apps
The app can draw windows over other apps, which can be abused for fake login screens.
Normal for chat bubbles, screen recorders and blue-light filters.
Not proven that it covers other apps.
Revoke it in Settings → Apps → Special access → Display over other apps if not needed.

string-array.name: risk_persistence
string-array.item: Runs in the background
The app can start again after the phone boots, or is exempt from battery optimisation.
Normal for messaging, alarm and sync apps.
Not proven that it keeps running.
Remove the battery exemption if the app does not need to run in the background.

string-array.name: risk_hidden_icon
string-array.item: No home screen icon
The app does not show in the app drawer, so it is easy to forget and harder to find for uninstalling.
Normal for keyboards, widgets, wallpapers and plug-ins opened from other apps.
Not known whether the icon is hidden on purpose.
Make sure you know what this app is. Uninstall it from Settings → Apps if you do not recognise it.

string-array.name: risk_install_apps
string-array.item: Installs other apps
The app can ask to install other APKs, which can be used to download additional apps.
Normal for app stores, file managers, browsers and backup tools such as PackPeek.
Android still asks before every install; not proven that it was used.
Do not allow \"Install unknown apps\" for apps you do not trust.

string-array.name: risk_all_files
string-array.item: All files access
The app can read and change every file in storage, including photos and documents.
Normal for file managers, antivirus and backup tools.
Not proven that files leave the device.
Revoke \"All files access\" if the app does not manage files.

string-array.name: risk_cleartext
string-array.item: Unencrypted traffic allowed
The app may communicate without encryption (HTTP), so others on the same Wi-Fi could read the data.
Sometimes needed for local devices such as printers or CCTV cameras.
Not proven that sensitive data is sent unencrypted.
Avoid logging in or paying through this app on public Wi-Fi.

string-array.name: risk_network_usage
string-array.item: Network data usage
Shows how much data the app used in the last 30 days, including while it was not open.
Background data is normal for sync, messaging and updates. Large amounts for an app you rarely use deserve a look.
These numbers do not show what the data was or where it went.
Restrict background data in Settings → Apps → Mobile data if the amount looks wrong.

string-array.name: risk_untrusted_signer
string-array.item: Unusual signing certificate
The app is signed with a debug certificate or a very recently created one, which is common for quickly built APKs outside official stores.
Normal for self-built apps, test builds or PackPeek merged .apk files.
Does not prove the app is harmful.
Make sure you trust where the file came from before installing it.

string-array.name: risk_data_theft
string-array.item: Personal data sent to a hidden destination

The app\'s own code reads personal data (such as SMS, contacts, notifications or screen text) and, in the same code path, sends data to a Telegram bot, a Discord webhook, or a public IP address written in the sending code. Scam apps use these channels because they need no named server that can be traced.

Ordinary apps send data to their own named servers, not to chat bots or webhooks. Developers sometimes use bots for crash reports, but those do not read personal data. A bare IP is a strong indicator only for a file or an app from an untrusted source; otherwise it needs attention.
Do not install this file. If it is installed: uninstall it, change passwords of accounts whose codes or messages it could read, and turn two-step verification back on.

string-array.name: risk_hidden_destination
string-array.item: Hidden destination in the code

The code contains the address of a Telegram bot, a Discord webhook or a public IP address without a domain name. Data sent there is hard to trace back to a company. Local addresses (home network, the device itself) are not counted.
Some apps use bots or webhooks for alerts, or reach their own servers by IP. It is a concern when combined with access to personal data.
Check whether the app needs to talk to chat services or raw IP addresses for its purpose. Prefer apps from known developers.

string-array.name: risk_call_forwarding
string-array.item: Call forwarding codes
The code contains phone codes that forward your calls (for example **21*) or sends USSD requests. Account thieves forward calls so voice OTP codes reach them instead of you.
Phone, carrier and call-management apps can use these codes legitimately.
Check your call forwarding settings (dial *#21#). Remove forwarding you did not set up, and uninstall the app if you do not recognise it.

string-array.name: risk_dynamic_code
string-array.item: Loads extra code
The app can load or run code that is not part of what was checked: a hidden DEX/APK inside the package, an encrypting packer or a class loader.
Large apps use dynamic loading for plug-ins and updates, and some companies protect their code with packers.
Treat the result of this check as incomplete for this app. Be cautious if the app also comes from outside an app store.

string-array.name: risk_shell_command
string-array.item: Runs shell commands
The code starts system commands (Runtime.exec or ProcessBuilder). Commands can read device information or logs, and on a rooted device do much more.
Crash reporters and device-info SDKs often run harmless commands such as getprop or logcat. It matters most when the app\'s own code does it.
Check whether the app needs this for its purpose. Be cautious if it also asks for root access or comes from outside an app store.

string-array.name: risk_clipboard
string-array.item: Reads the clipboard
The app can read text you copy, which may include passwords, OTP codes or account numbers.
Download and link-sharing apps often read the clipboard to pick up a copied link. Since Android 10 apps can only read it while they are on screen, and Android 12+ shows a notice.
Avoid copying passwords or OTP codes while this app is open.

string-array.name: risk_web_login
string-array.item: Reads WebView cookies
The app reads cookies from its built-in browser. Cookies can keep you logged in, so whoever holds them may act as you on that website.
Apps that let you log in to a website inside the app (for example to download your own posts) need cookies for that session.
Log in to important accounts only in their official app or browser. Log out and change the password if you are unsure.

string-array.name: risk_ad_sdks
string-array.item: Advertising and analytics SDKs
Third-party code that shows ads or measures how you use the app. These SDKs can collect device identifiers and usage data.
Very common in free apps; usually covered by the app\'s privacy policy.
Which data each SDK actually collects is not visible from the code check.
Check the Data safety section in Google Play and reset your advertising ID in Settings → Privacy → Ads if you like.

string-array.name: risk_destinations
string-array.item: Addresses in the code
Web addresses written in the app\'s own code: where the app is likely to connect.
Every connected app has these. Unknown domains are not suspicious by themselves.
Whether these addresses are contacted, and what is sent, is not visible from the code alone.
Look for addresses that do not match the app\'s developer, and for unencrypted http.

resources.string: Reads %1$s and sends to %2$s in the same code path (the value was not traced)
The value read from this data was traced into a call that sends it out (T3). It is still not proven that this path has run on your device; only watching the app while it runs could show that.
The code calls the functions this needs (T2), but no path that sends the data out was found. Code that never runs, or code loaded later, cannot be ruled out.
The app\'s own code was checked and does not call the functions this needs. Libraries or code loaded later could still use it.
Parts of the app could not be analysed (see Check coverage), so the code result may be incomplete.
